module_title: Gupta Empire and Harsha - Economy, Decline, Feudalism, and Inscriptions
introduction: At this advanced level, we will analyze the causes of the Gupta Empire's decline (like Huna invasions), the rise of Indian Feudalism through land grants, intricate economic details, and a deep dive into historical inscriptions.

core_concepts.title: Land Grants and the Rise of Feudalism
core_concepts.description: During the Gupta and Harsha periods, the practice of granting tax-free land (Agrahara) to Brahmins and temples increased significantly, leading to the rise of feudalism and the weakening of central authority.

core_concepts.title: The Huna Invasions
core_concepts.description: The Hunas, a Central Asian tribe, repeatedly attacked the Gupta Empire. Although Skandagupta successfully repelled them initially, continuous invasions eventually shattered the empire's economy.

core_concepts.title: Economy and Trade under Guptas
core_concepts.description: Trade with the West declined after the fall of the Roman Empire, but trade with South-East Asia surged. The Guptas issued the largest number of gold coins (Dinars), though their gold purity was lower than that of the Kushanas.

core_concepts.title: Prayag Prashasti (Allahabad Pillar Inscription)
core_concepts.description: Composed by Harisena, this inscription is the most authentic source of Samudragupta's conquests. It is engraved on the same Ashokan pillar that also carries inscriptions of Jahangir.

core_concepts.title: Aihole Inscription
core_concepts.description: Composed by Ravikirti, this inscription records the defeat of Harshavardhana by the Chalukyan king Pulakeshin II on the banks of the Narmada River, halting Harsha's southern expansion.

important_entities.name: Skandagupta
important_entities.significance: The Bhitari Pillar Inscription details his successful military campaigns against the Huna invaders.

important_entities.name: Pulakeshin II
important_entities.significance: The only king known to have definitively stopped the victorious march of Harshavardhana.

important_entities.name: Harisena
important_entities.key_fact: Court poet and Sandhivigrahika of Samudragupta
important_entities.significance: Composed the Prayag Prashasti, a prime example of the Champu style (mixture of prose and poetry) of Sanskrit literature.

important_entities.name: Dinar and Rupayaka
important_entities.significance: Dinars were gold coins, and Rupayaka were silver coins (issued by Chandragupta II after defeating the Shakas).

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.alert_title: Volume vs. Purity of Gold Coins
trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: The Guptas issued the 'highest number' of gold coins (Dinars), but the 'purest' gold coins in ancient India were issued by the Kushanas.
Often mistakenly linked to the Vedic period, the first archaeological evidence of the Sati practice is found in the Gupta period's 'Eran Inscription' (510 CE, Bhanugupta).

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Use 'EH' to remember Aihole Inscription is about Harsha's defeat, and 'BS' to remember Bhitari Inscription is about Skandagupta.
Helps recall that the first evidence of Sati is in Bhanugupta's 'Eran' inscription.

exam_strategy_tips: For UPSC and State PCS exams, prepare for analytical (statement-based) questions on the socio-economic impacts of 'Land Grants' and the origins of Indian Feudalism.
Rote learn the matching of various inscriptions (Prayag Prashasti, Aihole, Mehrauli Iron Pillar, Eran) with their respective composers and associated rulers.
